summary: Defines a simple challenge-response way to log in to IMAP mail servers, and the same idea works for POP. The server sends a changing challenge and the client proves it knows the password without sending the password itself. It replaces RFC 2095.

eli5.summary: The server asks a secret question that changes every time. You answer using your password but never say the password out loud, so eavesdroppers learn nothing useful.

questions: how does challenge response authentication work for imap
how is the cram-md5 digest calculated
subtitle: A simple login handshake for IMAP mail that proves you know the password without sending it.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 had strong authentication mechanisms that need a security infrastructure, or else a plain cleartext username and password. Nothing sat in between.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a one-time challenge. The client answers with its user name and a keyed MD5 digest of that challenge, computed with a shared secret.
tldr.outcome: The password never crosses the network and the server need not keep it in the clear, but the RFC itself calls the replay protection only conjectured and warns that a compromised server still exposes the secrets.

today: RFC 2195 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. It obsoletes RFC 2095, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CRAM Was Needed
sections.content:
IMAP4 offers an AUTHENTICATE command whose methods are meant to be extensible. The four methods in RFC 1731 are powerful but need some security infrastructure. The only other choice in IMAP is the LOGIN command, which presumably sends a cleartext username and password.

POP3 already had a lightweight challenge-response method called APOP, but APOP needs both client and server to hold the shared secret in cleartext. This RFC describes a mechanism similar to APOP and PPP CHAP that uses only MD5, in a keyed form, and avoids cleartext storage on the server. It can be used with IMAP and, in principle, with POP3.

It also does not require the server to keep per-login history, which would be hard for IMAP because several connections between one client and server may be open at about the same time.
sections.eli5: Mail programs could either use a very strong lock that is hard to set up, or just shout the password. This gives them a simple lock in the middle.

sections.title: The CRAM-MD5 Exchange
sections.content:
The authentication type is named CRAM-MD5. The server's first ready response carries a presumptively arbitrary string of random digits, a timestamp and the server's fully-qualified primary host name. In its unencoded form it must look like an RFC 822 msg-id.

The client replies with its user name, a space and a digest. The digest is the keyed MD5 of the timestamp (including the angle brackets), using the shared secret as the key. It is a 16-octet value sent in hexadecimal using lower-case ASCII characters.

The server checks the digest. If it is correct, the server should consider the client authenticated. Keyed MD5 is chosen because it gives greater security for short messages, and because precomputed intermediate results, called contexts, can be stored instead of the secret itself. CRAM does not support a protection mechanism, so the session after login is not protected by it.
sections.eli5: The server hands you a number that changes every time. You mix it with your secret in a special blender and hand back the result. The server mixes the same way and checks that the results match.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows CRAM inside the IMAP4 AUTHENTICATE command. The base64 encoding of challenges and responses belongs to that command, not to CRAM itself. In the example the shared secret is tanstaaftanstaaf and the challenge is the base64 form of <1896.697170952@postoffice.reston.mci.net>.

The resulting digest is b913a602c7eda7a495b4e6e7334d3890. The user name tim is put in front, and tim b913a602c7eda7a495b4e6e7334d3890 is base64 encoded for the reply. The secret is null-padded to a length of 64 bytes, and if it is longer than 64 bytes its MD5 digest is used as a 16 byte input instead.
sections.eli5: It is like a spy handshake: the guard says a code word, you reply with your name and a scrambled answer only you could make.

sections.title: Security Caveats
sections.content:
The RFC says it is conjectured that CRAM gives origin identification and replay protection for a session. A server that offers both a cleartext password command and this mechanism should not allow both methods of access for a given user.

Storing contexts on the server is only marginally better than storing secrets in cleartext, as CHAP and APOP require. It is not sufficient to protect the secrets if the server itself is compromised.
sections.eli5: The trick keeps eavesdroppers out, but if a burglar breaks into the server itself, the secrets can still be found.
